title: The Morning Brief: Djokovic exits US Open; Sabalenka advances; Orioles reach .500
dek: Tennis and baseball saw major shifts on the US Open's opening day and in the regular season stretch. Djokovic fell in the first round for the first time at Flushing Meadows, while administrative upheaval continued in college sports.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: Djokovic's first-round loss to world No. 49 Mariano Navone on August 31 marks his first opening-round exit at a Grand Slam since 2006 and removes a major contender from a US Open reshaped by Sinner's injury absence and Alcaraz's wrist recovery.
bottom_line: Tuesday saw major upheaval across tennis, golf, baseball, and college sports. Djokovic's first-round exit reshapes the US Open men's draw; the PGA Tour's new betting-monitoring programs debut in 2027; the Orioles chase a wild-card berth with new depth; and UCLA's third major leadership reset in one year raises questions about structural spending control. The coming days will test whether Djokovic's absence opens the field, whether Sabalenka sustains her title defense, and whether the Orioles' September stretch reaches October.
body: Novak Djokovic's 20-year streak at the US Open ended on August 31 when he lost to Mariano Navone 7-6 (7-5) 5-7 4-6 6-2 6-1 in the first round, his first opening-round exit at Flushing Meadows and his first Grand Slam first-round loss since 2006. The 39-year-old displayed visible signs of distress throughout the four-hour-36-minute match, vomiting multiple times and using an inhaler during breaks. After the loss, Djokovic said he has dealt with health issues "pretty much every match this year," citing heat and humidity as aggravating factors; the nature of his recurring condition remains undisclosed. The defeat ends his pursuit of a standalone record 25th Grand Slam title, moving him clear of Margaret Court's 24.

The tournament's shape shifted with Djokovic's exit. World No. 1 Jannik Sinner is absent through injury, and defending champion Carlos Alcaraz is returning from a long-term wrist injury. On the women's side, Aryna Sabalenka advanced with a 6-2, 6-4 victory over Camila Osorio on August 31, opening her bid for a third consecutive US Open title. Elena Rybakina sits at No. 1 in the live rankings; Sabalenka must win the title to retain any hope of holding the top ranking. Rybakina will become the new No. 1 if she reaches the semifinals, regardless of other results.

Off the court, the PGA Tour announced new security measures for 2027 in response to betting-related fan interference during play. Senior VP Andy Levinson said the Tour is "concerned about fans interacting with our players in a negative manner, and certainly the potential for fans to try to impact the competition in some way." The Tour will deploy volunteer ambassadors trained to identify disruptive behavior and monitor online harassment. PGA Tour VP Scott Warfield noted that less than 5% of ejections in 2026 stemmed from betting-related incidents but said "one is one too many for us." The Tour has declined to partner with prediction markets as of 2026, citing regulatory uncertainty, while the MLB, NHL, and USTA have signed such agreements.

In baseball, the Baltimore Orioles claimed outfielder Luis Robert Jr., 29, off outright waivers from the Mets on August 31 as they pursue a September postseason push. The Orioles sit one game behind the Guardians for a wild-card berth despite carrying a sub-.500 record. Robert Jr. did not report to the Mets before being placed on waivers; the circumstances remain unclear, as does whether he will join the Orioles' roster. On the field, Colton Cowser made a leaping home-run robbery at Coors Field to end the game and lift Baltimore to .500 for the first time since April.

Curaçao won the 2026 Little League World Series championship on August 31, defeating Paseo Verde Little League of Henderson, Nevada 11-2. The victory marks Curaçao's second title in tournament history, underscoring the Caribbean nation's emerging footprint in youth baseball's most prominent international stage.

In college athletics, UCLA fired Athletic Director Martin Jarmond on September 1 and paid him a $6.5 million buyout, citing a significant financial deficit in the athletic department. The departure comes days before new football coach Bob Chesney's debut and follows the firing of former head coach DeShaun Foster earlier in the year. Foster's exit carried a larger buyout, leaving total leadership turnover costs exceeding $12 million in one year. The SEC, meanwhile, announced it will challenge a Louisiana court order that would allow former NFL players to compete in college sports, defending its right to enforce rules against athletes who have signed professional contracts.
